questions.q: A 35-year-old man presents with a painless, indurated ulcer on the glans penis for 3 weeks. Inguinal lymph nodes are enlarged, non-tender, and rubbery. Dark-field microscopy of the exudate reveals motile spirochetes. Which organism is responsible?
questions.exp: Painless indurated ulcer (chancre) with non-tender lymphadenopathy and motile spirochetes on dark-field microscopy is classic for primary syphilis caused by Treponema pallidum. Haemophilus ducreyi causes painful soft chancroid; Chlamydia trachomatis causes lymphogranuloma venereum with groove sign.

questions.q: A 28-year-old woman develops multiple painful, tender ulcers on the labia with a soft, undermined base and associated ipsilateral tender inguinal lymphadenopathy (bubo). Gram stain of the pus shows 'school of fish' pattern. Which antibiotic is the first-line treatment?
questions.exp: Painful soft ulcers with undermined edges and the 'school of fish' (strepto-bacilli in chains) on Gram stain indicates chancroid (H. ducreyi). Azithromycin 1g single dose is first-line. Ciprofloxacin 500 mg BD x 3 days is an alternative.

questions.q: A 22-year-old man presents with a non-tender swelling in the right inguinal region. On examination there is a groove above and below the Poupart's ligament — the 'groove sign'. The most likely diagnosis is:
questions.exp: The 'groove sign of Greenblatt' — inguinal lymphadenopathy divided by the inguinal ligament — is pathognomonic of lymphogranuloma venereum (LGV) caused by Chlamydia trachomatis serovars L1-L3. Treatment is doxycycline 100 mg BD for 21 days.

questions.q: A 40-year-old man from rural India presents with beefy-red, painless, hypertrophied granulomatous ulcers on the genitals. Punch biopsy shows large macrophages containing intracytoplasmic Donovan bodies (safety-pin appearance). The causative organism is:
questions.exp: Granuloma inguinale (donovanosis) is caused by Klebsiella granulomatis (formerly Calymmatobacterium granulomatis). Donovan bodies are intracytoplasmic inclusions in large mononuclear cells on Giemsa stain. Treatment: azithromycin or doxycycline for at least 3 weeks.

questions.q: A 7-year-old child presents with honey-coloured crusted lesions around the nose and mouth. Culture grows beta-haemolytic Streptococcus. Which complication is this child at highest risk for?
questions.exp: Impetigo caused by nephritogenic strains of Group A Streptococcus (GAS) can lead to acute post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis (APSGN). Unlike pharyngeal GAS infection, cutaneous GAS does NOT cause rheumatic fever. Treatment with antibiotics does not prevent APSGN once established.

questions.q: A 55-year-old diabetic man develops a rapidly spreading, necrotizing infection of the scrotum with crepitus and black necrotic skin. He is febrile and toxic. The most appropriate immediate management is:
opts: Urgent surgical debridement with broad-spectrum antibiotics
questions.exp: This is Fournier's gangrene — polymicrobial necrotizing fasciitis of the perineum/scrotum. The mainstay of treatment is urgent wide surgical debridement combined with broad-spectrum IV antibiotics. Delayed surgery is a key predictor of mortality. Hyperbaric oxygen is an adjunct, not primary treatment.

questions.q: A patient with leprosy presents with sudden onset of painful erythematous nodules over the face, trunk, and extremities associated with fever, malaise, iritis, and orchitis. Skin biopsy shows panniculitis with neutrophilic infiltrate and no foamy macrophages. This reaction is:
questions.exp: Erythema Nodosum Leprosum (ENL) is a Type 2 lepra reaction occurring in lepromatous and borderline lepromatous leprosy. It is an immune complex–mediated (Type III) reaction with systemic features (fever, orchitis, iritis, neuritis). Histology shows panniculitis with neutrophil infiltration. Treatment: thalidomide or prednisolone.

questions.q: A patient with borderline tuberculoid (BT) leprosy shows sudden upgrading of a skin patch with increased erythema and edema, and a new painful nerve thickening over 2 days. This is best classified as:
questions.exp: Type 1 (reversal) reaction is a delayed-type hypersensitivity (Type IV) reaction occurring in borderline leprosy (BT, BB, BL). It presents with upgrading of lesions (acute inflammation of existing patches) and acute neuritis. Lucio's phenomenon occurs only in lepromatous leprosy in Mexico/Caribbean. Management: prednisolone.

questions.q: A 45-year-old woman with multibacillary leprosy develops painless, non-healing, trophic ulcer on the right sole. Examination shows loss of pain and temperature sensation in a 'stocking' distribution. The nerve most commonly involved in foot involvement in leprosy is:
questions.exp: The posterior tibial nerve is the most commonly involved nerve causing plantar anaesthesia and trophic ulcers (Planter involvement) in leprosy. Common peroneal nerve involvement causes foot drop. Ulnar nerve involvement (most common nerve affected overall) causes claw hand (4th and 5th fingers).

questions.q: A 30-year-old immunocompetent man develops grouped vesicles on an erythematous base on the right side of his forehead and nose tip. He has intense pain and photophobia in the right eye. The most likely diagnosis is:
opts: Herpes zoster ophthalmicus with Hutchinson's sign
questions.exp: Nasociliary branch involvement in herpes zoster ophthalmicus produces vesicles on the nose tip — Hutchinson's sign — which predicts a high risk of ocular involvement (keratitis, uveitis). The nasociliary nerve also supplies the eye. Treatment: acyclovir 800 mg 5 times/day for 7 days + ophthalmology referral.

questions.q: A 2-year-old child has an eruption of hundreds of intensely pruritic vesicles all over the body in crops over 5 days. New crops keep appearing while older ones crust. A pathognomonic finding on Tzanck smear would be:
questions.exp: Varicella (chickenpox) caused by VZV shows multinucleated giant cells (ballooning degeneration) on Tzanck smear. This is also seen in herpes simplex. Acantholytic cells are seen in pemphigus vulgaris. The distribution of crops in various stages (new vesicles + crusted lesions simultaneously) is characteristic of varicella.

questions.q: A 25-year-old male presents with a single, pearly, dome-shaped papule with central umbilication on his trunk. On expression, a cheesy material comes out. Microscopy of this material reveals:
questions.exp: Molluscum contagiosum (poxvirus) presents as umbilicated pearly papules. Expressed material shows Henderson-Patterson bodies (large eosinophilic intracytoplasmic inclusion bodies that displace the nucleus) on Giemsa or H&E staining. Negri bodies are seen in rabies (neuronal); Cowdry A inclusions in HSV-infected cells.

questions.q: A 50-year-old renal transplant recipient on cyclosporine develops multiple pigmented, verrucous plaques on sun-exposed areas. Biopsy shows acanthosis, papillomatosis, and koilocytes. The most likely causative agent is:
questions.exp: Epidermodysplasia verruciformis (EV)-like eruptions in immunosuppressed patients are caused by beta-HPV types (HPV 5, 8). Koilocytes (vacuolated cells with pyknotic nuclei) are hallmarks of HPV infection. These lesions carry risk of squamous cell carcinoma on sun exposure. Merkel cell polyomavirus causes Merkel cell carcinoma.

questions.q: A 35-year-old woman presents with widespread erythema, large flaccid bullae, and positive Nikolsky sign involving >30% BSA following carbamazepine use. Mucosal involvement is severe with pseudomembranous conjunctivitis. The most likely diagnosis is:
questions.exp: TEN (Lyell syndrome) involves >30% BSA skin detachment caused by drug hypersensitivity. Causative drugs: anticonvulsants, sulfonamides, allopurinol, NSAIDs. Severity is assessed by SCORTEN score. SJS involves <10% BSA; overlap SJS-TEN: 10-30%. SSSS in adults is very rare; cleavage is at the granular layer (subcorneal), not full-thickness epidermal necrosis.

questions.q: A 60-year-old woman presents with chronic recurrent painful oral erosions and flaccid bullae on the trunk. Nikolsky sign is positive. Histopathology shows suprabasal acantholysis with 'tombstone' basal cells. DIF shows IgG and C3 in a 'chicken-wire' (fishnet) pattern on keratinocyte cell surfaces. The diagnosis is:
questions.exp: Pemphigus vulgaris: suprabasal acantholysis, tombstone sign (basal cells remain attached to basement membrane), IgG antibodies against desmoglein 3 (mucosal) and desmoglein 1 (cutaneous). DIF shows IgG in intercellular spaces in a fishnet pattern. Nikolsky sign is positive. Bullous pemphigoid shows subepidermal cleavage with eosinophils and linear IgG/C3 at BMZ.

questions.q: A 70-year-old man develops intensely pruritic tense bullae on erythematous/urticarial plaques on the trunk and flexures. Nikolsky sign is negative. DIF shows linear IgG and C3 at the dermoepidermal junction. ELISA is positive for anti-BP180 and anti-BP230 antibodies. The diagnosis is:
questions.exp: Bullous pemphigoid: subepidermal bullae with eosinophilic infiltrate, tense bullae (hard to rupture), negative Nikolsky sign, linear IgG/C3 at BMZ on DIF. Antibodies are against BP180 (type XVII collagen) and BP230 (plectin). First-line: topical or oral corticosteroids. EBA has a similar DIF but shows IgG at the dermal side of salt-split skin.

questions.q: A 25-year-old man with coeliac disease develops intensely pruritic, grouped papulovesicles on the elbows, knees, and buttocks. Skin biopsy shows neutrophilic microabscesses at the dermal papillae tips. DIF shows granular IgA deposits at the papillary dermis. The treatment of choice is:
questions.exp: Dermatitis herpetiformis (DH) is associated with coeliac disease (gluten-sensitive enteropathy). DIF shows granular IgA at papillary dermal tips (pathognomonic). Treatment: dapsone for rapid symptom relief AND strict gluten-free diet (disease control). Linear IgA disease shows linear IgA on DIF.

questions.q: A 40-year-old woman presents with photosensitivity, malar rash, arthritis, and oral ulcers. ANA is positive at 1:640 (speckled pattern). Anti-dsDNA and anti-Smith antibodies are positive. Skin biopsy of sun-exposed and sun-protected skin shows IgG deposition at BMZ on DIF ('lupus band test'). The most likely diagnosis is:
questions.exp: SLE: positive lupus band test (IgG at BMZ) in both sun-exposed and non-sun-exposed skin (characteristic of SLE vs. discoid LE where it is only in sun-exposed). Anti-dsDNA and anti-Smith are specific for SLE. SCLE is associated with anti-Ro/SSA and anti-La/SSB. Dermatomyositis shows Gottron's papules and heliotrope rash.

questions.q: A 45-year-old woman presents with Raynaud's phenomenon, skin tightening of the fingers and face, telangiectasias, calcinosis, and dysphagia. Serology shows positive anti-centromere antibodies. Which organ complication is this patient at risk for?
questions.exp: The CREST syndrome (Calcinosis, Raynaud's, Esophageal dysmotility, Sclerodactyly, Telangiectasia) is limited systemic sclerosis associated with anti-centromere antibodies and increased risk of pulmonary arterial hypertension. Diffuse SSc (anti-Scl-70 antibodies) is more associated with pulmonary fibrosis and renal crisis.

questions.q: A 35-year-old woman develops proximal muscle weakness, Gottron's papules over MCP/PIP joints, and heliotrope rash. CPK is markedly elevated. Anti-Jo-1 antibodies are positive. What is the most important systemic complication to screen for?
questions.exp: Anti-Jo-1 (anti-histidyl tRNA synthetase) is an antisynthetase antibody associated with antisynthetase syndrome: inflammatory myopathy + interstitial lung disease (ILD) + mechanic's hands + Raynaud's + arthritis. ILD is the most important complication and the leading cause of morbidity/mortality. Regular pulmonary function tests and HRCT chest screening is mandatory.

questions.q: A 65-year-old fair-skinned man with lifelong sun exposure presents with a pearly papule with rolled edges and telangiectasias on the nose. Central ulceration develops over months. The most likely diagnosis is:
questions.exp: Basal cell carcinoma (BCC) — most common skin cancer. Nodular BCC: pearly papule with telangiectasias, rolled border, and central ulceration ('rodent ulcer'). Occurs on sun-exposed skin (nose, face). Risk factors: UV exposure, fair skin (Fitzpatrick I/II), arsenic, xeroderma pigmentosum. Treatment: excision, Mohs surgery, or topical imiquimod.

questions.q: A 70-year-old farmer presents with a rapidly growing, crater-like nodule on the dorsum of the hand with a keratinous plug in the centre, which appeared over 6-8 weeks. The most likely diagnosis is:
questions.exp: Keratoacanthoma (KA) is a rapidly growing (weeks), self-involuting nodule with a central keratin-filled crater. It typically appears on sun-exposed skin in elderly men and may spontaneously resolve in 3-6 months. Histologically identical to well-differentiated SCC in some cases ('KA-type SCC'). Treatment: excision to confirm diagnosis and prevent rare malignant transformation.

questions.q: A 50-year-old man with a history of immunosuppression post-renal transplant presents with a violaceous nodule on the leg. Biopsy shows spindle cell proliferation with vascular slits and extravasated red blood cells. The causative virus is:
questions.exp: Kaposi's sarcoma is caused by Human Herpesvirus 8 (HHV-8 / KSHV). Spindle cells and vascular slits are histological hallmarks. Classical KS (elderly Mediterranean men) vs. AIDS-related KS vs. iatrogenic/transplant KS. Treatment: reduction of immunosuppression, antiretroviral therapy in HIV, local (radiation, cryotherapy) or systemic chemotherapy (liposomal doxorubicin).

questions.q: A 55-year-old man presents with a slowly enlarging, darkly pigmented macule on the sole of the foot with irregular border and colour variation (tan, brown, black). Dermoscopy shows a parallel ridge pattern. The most likely diagnosis is:
questions.exp: Acral lentiginous melanoma (ALM) is the most common melanoma subtype in dark-skinned individuals, occurring on palms, soles, and subungual regions. Dermoscopic 'parallel ridge pattern' (pigment on ridges, not furrows) is characteristic and differentiates ALM from benign acral naevi (parallel furrow pattern). Prompt excision with wide margins is required.

questions.q: A patient with a tinea capitis infection is found to have fluorescence under Wood's lamp. The most likely causative organism is:
questions.exp: Microsporum species (M. canis, M. audouinii) fluoresce green under Wood's lamp due to pteridine production (ectothrix infection with fluorescent hyphae). Trichophyton species (T. tonsurans, T. violaceum) are non-fluorescent. Trichophyton schoenleinii causes favus and shows faint bluish-green fluorescence. T. tonsurans is the most common cause of black-dot tinea capitis.

questions.q: A 30-year-old immunocompetent man from Maharashtra presents with a verrucous plaque on the foot with black grain discharge from sinuses. KOH mount shows brown, thick-walled, muriform (sclerotic) cells. The diagnosis is:
questions.exp: Chromoblastomycosis is caused by dematiaceous (melanised) fungi (Fonsecaea pedrosoi, Cladophialophora carrionii). Classic histopathology: muriform cells (Medlar bodies / copper-pennies) — brown, thick-walled, septate sclerotic cells in tissue. Mycetoma has grains in sinuses; sporotrichosis has a lymphocutaneous pattern; lobomycosis (Lacazia loboi) has chain-forming, non-culturable yeast-like cells.

questions.q: A 35-year-old man with advanced HIV (CD4 count 50 cells/μL) develops disseminated papules resembling molluscum contagiosum on his face and trunk. India ink preparation of CSF shows encapsulated yeast. Serum and CSF cryptococcal antigen is positive. The most appropriate treatment is:
opts: Amphotericin B + flucytosine induction, then fluconazole consolidation
questions.exp: Cryptococcal meningoencephalitis in HIV: standard treatment is amphotericin B deoxycholate (or liposomal AmB) + flucytosine for 2-week induction, followed by fluconazole 400 mg/day consolidation (8 weeks), then fluconazole 200 mg/day maintenance until CD4 >200. Skin lesions mimicking molluscum are a clue to disseminated cryptococcosis.

questions.q: A 20-year-old woman presents with widespread silvery-white scales on erythematous plaques over scalp, elbows, and knees. There is nail pitting and onycholysis. Her mother has a similar condition. The most likely HLA association is:
questions.exp: Psoriasis vulgaris is most strongly associated with HLA-Cw6 (also written HLA-C*06:02). Patients with HLA-Cw6 have earlier onset (type I psoriasis), more severe disease, and better response to biologics. HLA-B27 is associated with psoriatic arthritis and ankylosing spondylitis. HLA-DR3 and DQ2 are associated with coeliac disease and DH.

questions.q: A 45-year-old man on methotrexate for psoriasis develops nausea, mouth ulcers, and macrocytic anaemia. The mechanism of methotrexate toxicity in this context is:
opts: Inhibition of dihydrofolate reductase leading to folate deficiency
Direct toxicity to GI mucosa via alkylation
questions.exp: Methotrexate inhibits dihydrofolate reductase (DHFR), blocking conversion of dihydrofolate to tetrahydrofolate, leading to functional folate deficiency. This causes mucosal ulceration, pancytopenia, and macrocytic anaemia. Folic acid supplementation (5 mg/week, not on MTX day) reduces toxicity without affecting efficacy. Regular CBC and LFT monitoring is mandatory.

questions.q: A 40-year-old patient with chronic urticaria has not responded to twice-daily second-generation antihistamines for 4 weeks. The next step in management per current guidelines is:
opts: Add a first-generation antihistamine at night
Updose second-generation antihistamine to 4× standard dose
questions.exp: Per EAACI/GA2LEN/EDF/WAO chronic urticaria guidelines, the stepwise approach is: Step 1: standard-dose second-generation H1 antihistamine → Step 2: updose antihistamine up to 4× → Step 3: add omalizumab → Step 4: add cyclosporin. First-generation antihistamines have significant sedation and anticholinergic side effects and are not preferred. Systemic corticosteroids are only for acute exacerbations, not chronic use.

questions.q: A 28-year-old woman presents with vitiligo affecting 20% of her body surface area. She wants the fastest repigmentation. Which light-based therapy has the highest evidence for focal/segmental vitiligo?
questions.exp: Excimer laser (308 nm monochromatic light) provides targeted, high-dose UVB to focal areas of vitiligo with good repigmentation rates (especially for segmental vitiligo) and fewer sessions than NB-UVB. NB-UVB (311-313 nm) is preferred for widespread disease and is the gold-standard phototherapy. PUVA is less preferred due to carcinogenicity and systemic psoralen side effects. Broadband UVB is largely replaced by NB-UVB.
